about: The words of the chain walrus_ivory (Data/encounters/chain_walrus_ivory_793.json; Design/content/chains/walrus_ivory.md): walrus ivory and hide rope from the far north, as Ohthere told King Alfred about 890. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the six news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Ohthere and Wulfstan are real and are named; King Alfred is real, is called 'the king', and his words are invented; everyone else is an ordinary invented person whom the forge names. Nothing is quoted from a translation: what Ohthere says of the teeth, the rope, the Finnas' dues, his deer, the days of sail and the Beormas follows his report in the Old English Orosius (texts_793.json ohthere; Bosworth 1859, Sweet 1883) in our own plain rendering, and Wulfstan's line follows his (texts_793.json wulfstan). The line the priest reads in s14 is the report's opening in our rendering. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Teeth on the jetty
A ship from the far north lies at the jetty, a month's sail behind her. Her master has laid out long yellow teeth and coils of dark rope, and nobody here can tell him what they fetch in the south.
You are from the south. Good. I have come a month along the land, and every man here tells me the price in his own harbour, which I know already.
The southerner again. I have not sold them. Nobody here has told me anything new since you went by.
Teeth of the horse-whale. He is not a big whale, seven ells at the most. But the bone in his teeth is noble, and his hide makes the best ship's rope there is.
I am Ohthere. I live northmost of all Northmen. I say so because I went and looked. North of me there is waste, and Finnas who hunt and fish.
I am told the Christians carve their god out of tooth. I have not seen it. Have you?
Ask what he wants of a southerner
Tell him plainly what tooth fetches in the south
Wish him a good market and go by
He looks at you for some time, as a man looks at a sky. Then he picks up a coil of rope and walks to the boat shed, and plainly you are to follow.
You tell him what you have seen: a bishop's staff, a book cover, and that the great tooth from the south comes seldom now and costs gold. He has you say it twice. He does not write, so he listens.
He nods. He has a month's sail home in front of him and is in no hurry about one afternoon. The teeth are still on the jetty when you go back to the ship.
What the Finnas pay
In the boat shed he shows you the year's tribute laid out by kind, and tells you what each man of the Finnas owes him. Then he says what he wants.
Each pays by his birth. The best-born pays fifteen marten skins, five reindeer, one bear skin, ten measures of feathers, a coat of bear skin or otter, and two ship's ropes.
Each rope sixty ells. One of whale's hide, one of seal's. Cut round and round the beast in one strip. Pull on it. Harder.
I have six hundred deer, tame, and six more that draw the wild ones in. Also twenty cattle, twenty sheep and twenty pigs. In the south that is a poor man. I know it.
You told me a price before I asked you to buy. That is not how it is done in harbours. I noticed it.
I want one man who has stood in a southern market with one of these in his hand. Take a pair. Show them where teeth are carved. Then tell me what you saw. Not what you were told.
I come down the coast again after midsummer. The king's farm on the Karmsund is on my way. Look for me there.
Take a pair on his trust
Pay him for the pair, and owe nothing
Take the rope and carry only the question
He puts the pair in your hands and a coil of rope on top. No witness, no tally stick. He says the rope is not trade, it is manners, and the teeth are his until he hears what they fetched.
He weighs your silver twice on his own scale and once on yours. The pair is yours now, and he adds a coil of rope, which he says is not trade but manners.
He shrugs and gives you a coil of rope anyway, so that the south may at least pull on something. The question goes with you. The teeth stay in the shed.
The comb-maker's saw
A comb-maker at Sliesthorp works antler from first light to dark. He takes the tooth in both hands and turns it to the light before he says anything.
Horse-whale. I get one in three years, and never a pair. Who sent you?
Look at the broken end. Outside it is white and close, like the best bone. Inside it is clouded, like curds. A carver keeps his figures in the white. So the thick teeth are the dear ones.
The Christians' priests ask for it. They want it white and broad, for the boards of their books. The great tooth from the south does not come any more, they say. I am only told this.
For this pair I give silver to the weight of a hundred and ten pennies, cut and weighed here. A priest's carver on the Rhine would give more, and take until Yule to do it.
The pair is Ohthere's until he has heard what it fetched. He did not say you could not sell it. He said he wanted to know.
Sell him the pair for weighed silver
Pay him to cut a gaming king from the tip
Thank him and keep the pair whole
He cuts hack silver into the pan until the beam is level, and then puts in one more sliver, for the pair. He carries the teeth to the back of the shed himself and does not let the boy touch them.
He saws a thumb's length off the tip and by evening it is a small king with his hands on his knees and a beard like a spade. The tooth is shorter. The king goes in your purse.
He gives the tooth back slowly. He says that if you change your mind he is here every day but the day they bury him.
A tooth on the reeve's table
Since the king took London the trade is moving inside the old walls. The reeve who sees to the landing has a clerk beside him, and the clerk has seen ivory before. Neither has seen this.
It is not elephant. I have handled elephant, on a bishop's staff. What beast is it, and who kills it?
The king asks every stranger about his own country. Franks, Frisians, Bretons, heathen men too. He would sooner hear a hunter than a flatterer, and he gets more flatterers.
Our carvers cut whale's bone, because there is nothing better to be had. A book board in this would be asked for by every minster in the kingdom, and by two I can think of across the sea.
A heathen from north of everything, you say. Heathen men have come up this river before. They did not come to sell.
This small king is cut from it? Leave him with me until evening. There is a man I want to see him.
A rope of hide that held when the bast parted. The king has ships at sea every summer. Say that part again, slowly.
Ask the king's peace for the Northman to come himself
Ask to be the man who brings the teeth
Ask only what the king's goldsmith would pay

The reeve does not say yes. He has the clerk write that a Frisian asked the king's peace for a Northman of the far north with teeth to sell, and the day. In this town a thing written down is half granted.
The reeve says the king does not much care who brings a thing so long as it comes. He orders four pairs against next year at a good price, and asks no more about the man who hunts them.
The goldsmith is sent for. He names a price, then looks at the tooth again and names a better one. By evening the Strand has heard there is a new kind of ivory, and nobody has any.
The halyard parts
A squall comes down out of a clear sky. The bast halyard strands at the masthead and the yard hangs by what is left of it. The coil of hide rope lies under the thwart.
The steersman looks at the masthead and then at the coil. He says nothing. He is a man with opinions about new rope.
Hide rope wants grease, the Northman said, or it goes slack when it has been wet a long time. It need not be a long time.
Reeve the hide rope and hoist on it
Knot the bast and keep the hide rope to sell
Lower the yard and ride it out

The yard goes up on the dark rope and stays up. The squall leans on it for an hour and goes away. The steersman greases the rope that evening without being asked, which is the nearest he comes to praise.
The knot holds. The sail sets a hand lower than it should for the rest of the passage, and the coil stays dry under the thwart, worth what it was worth.
The knot draws through the block and the yard comes down across the thwarts. A man has a split scalp and nobody has much to say to you. The coil is still under the thwart, quite unharmed.
You get the yard down before it falls and lie to the sea with the sail bundled. It blows itself out by dark. Half a day lost, and the halyard to splice in the morning.
Held at the sound
Ohthere's ship lies under the king's farm with her sail carried ashore. The king's steward says the tribute of the Finnas is the king's to share out, not a Halogalander's to sell.
King Harald has the land now, from the Vik northward. What the Finnas pay, they pay to the man the king names. I have not heard him name this one.
My father took that tribute, and his father. I did not hear that any king came north to help them carry it.
Four ounces of silver for the sound, and he has his sail back. Or he waits for the king, who is at another farm. The king may come before the snow.
You came. Good. Tell me what the tooth fetched. After that, tell me whether you know how a man talks to a steward.
A hundred and ten pennies' weight at Sliesthorp, for one pair. Then a steward's four ounces is not much. I will remember who told me.
You have been in the south with one of those teeth. I would like to know what it is the king lets sail past his own door.
Lay down the four ounces for him
Speak for him before the men of the sound
Tell the steward what the teeth are worth
Wait with him until the steward tires

The steward weighs the silver and has the sail carried down. Ohthere does not thank you. He puts two pairs of teeth in your boat while you are looking the other way, and says the Heaths are five days from Skiringssal and he will be there.

You say that a due is owed on what passes the sound, and a tribute is not a cargo until it is sold. The farmers like it. They pay the steward too. He gives the sail back with a face like a shut door. Ohthere says he will be at the Heaths.

You speak well and in the wrong tongue, and the farmers laugh in the wrong places. The steward halves the due to be rid of the noise, and you pay it. Ohthere says a bad speech for a man is still a speech for him. He will be at the Heaths.

You tell the steward what a comb-maker gives and what a king's goldsmith would. He counts on his fingers and stops. Ohthere's cargo is carried up to the king's shed. Ohthere watches you from his own deck and says nothing at all.

Nine days. Ohthere mends a strap, then every strap. On the tenth day the steward wants the beach for another ship and has the sail carried down unpaid. Ohthere says he will be at the Heaths, and that you wait well for a southerner.
A sail from the islands

Two days out, with Denmark to port, a long ship comes out from behind an island under oars. She has seen two laden hulls and no shields. Ohthere's ship is a bowshot ahead of you, and she is the slower.
Twenty oars or more. They are not hurrying yet.
Ohthere's steersman holds a spear up flat, points it at you and then at the water beside him. It is a question.
Two traders and only one of me. Heave to, and we shall see which of you is the open-handed one.
Close up beside Ohthere and show iron
Run inside the islands where she cannot follow
Heave to and pay them

Two hulls side by side, a spear at every thwart, and Ohthere's men hunt whales for their living. The long ship rows a wide ring round you, twice, and goes back behind her island. Nobody was open-handed.

They come on anyway, and for the time it takes to say a prayer it is oars and axes over the rail. Then they find the hide rope will not cut and the whale hunters will not give way, and they leave with a purse and a bloody nose. You have your own to bind up.
You put the helm over for the gap between two islands where the water goes pale. Ohthere follows your wake without a question. The long ship draws too much, and knows it, and stops.

The gap is narrower than it looked and the wind dies under the land. They come up with you on oars, cheerful, and take what is nearest to hand. Ohthere, who followed you in, loses a bundle of skins and does not mention it.
You heave to and count silver into a shield held out on an oar. The man with the shield bites one piece, nods, and wishes you a fair wind. Ohthere's ship waits a bowshot off until it is done.
At the Heaths

Five days from Skiringssal, and the jetties of the market at the head of the fjord. Ohthere has never been further south than this. A skipper who knows the eastern sea is drinking with him, and a Frisian from the Rhine has already asked the price of the whole cargo.
Five days. Three with Denmark on the left hand and open sea on the right. Two with the islands on the left. I say it so that you can say it after me.
And on the second day a long ship, which went home. You came up beside me when you could have gone on. I counted that too.
I am Wulfstan. I ran from here to Truso in seven days and nights, and the ship was under sail the whole way. Wendland on the right hand as far as the mouth of the Vistula.
The king of the West Saxons will sit a whole evening for a thing like that. I have seen him do it. He asks which hand the land was on, and he knows if you guess.
The Frisian's silver is on the scale now. The English king's is across a sea I do not know. One of those is nearer. I have not decided that nearer is better.
Lay your goods with mine and we share what comes back. Or pilot me for a tenth. Or take the teeth up the Rhine yourself, and I go home. Choose. I have deer to see to.
Lay three hundred pennies in with his goods and sail for England
Pilot him to England for a tenth
Buy the teeth outright for the Rhine
Carry the teeth up the Rhine on shares

Your silver goes into his chest and his hand into yours, in front of Wulfstan, who says he has witnessed worse bargains sober. From here you sail ahead and Ohthere follows. By the fifth evening you understand half of what his men shout at each other.

A tenth, then, and no silver of yours at risk. You sail ahead and he follows, a bowshot astern, the whole way down the Frisian shore. By the fifth evening you understand half of what his men shout at each other.

He weighs your silver and has the teeth carried across to you in two chests, tied with his own rope and his own knot. He sails north the next morning. He says the English king will have to find out about the north some other way.

Two chests come across to your hold, tied with his own knot, and half of what they fetch is to lie for him with the Frisian here by next summer. He sails north in the morning. He does not look like a man who expects to be cheated, which is a hard thing to cheat.
A heathen at the hythe

Ohthere's ship lies off the hythe inside the walls. The reeve will let the teeth land. The priest beside him says a heathen who has not so much as been signed with the cross does not sit down at a Christian king's table.
Let him take the first signing. It is not baptism. It is a cross on the forehead and a few words, and after it he may eat with Christian men. Merchants do it in every northern harbour.
I have been told about this signing. I am told it does no harm. I have not been told that it does my deer any good.
Or a man the town knows swears for him: that he comes in peace, and that any harm he does is paid out of the swearer's purse.
You asked the king's peace for him a year ago. I had it written down. That counts for something, even with a priest.
Or you go in with the teeth and my words. You have heard them often enough. I can mend a strap here as well as anywhere.
Swear for him yourself
Ask him to take the signing
Go in alone with his teeth and his words

You swear it on the reeve's relics: his peace, your purse. The priest says an oath for a heathen is still an oath, and that he will be watching the heathen. Ohthere is to come ashore in three days, when the king sits.
He stands still for it like a horse being shod. Afterwards he asks whether it wears off in salt water. The priest, who has done this before, says only if he wants it to. The king sits in three days.
The teeth go ashore in two chests. Ohthere sits down on his own thwart with a strap across his knee and does not watch you go. The king sits in three days.
He said to his lord
The king sits with a clerk at his elbow and the teeth on the board in front of him. He does not ask the price. He asks how far north the land goes, and whether any man lives beyond the waste.
I wished to know that myself. So I sailed north three days with the waste on the right hand and the open sea on the left. Then I was as far as the whale hunters go. Then three days more.
The Beormas told me many things about their land and the lands about it. I do not know what is true in them, because I did not see it.
Sixty in two days, with five other men. Say the number again for my clerk. He has stopped writing.
Sixty. With five others. I was there.
And the hide rope held when this man's bast parted? Then I want rope before I want teeth.
This small king was cut from one of these teeth, they tell me. I wondered what kind of man brings in the beast he is made of. A quiet one, it seems.
He says 'I do not know' more often than any man I have ever written down. The king likes him for it.
And you brought him. What does a man want, who carries another man's story across the sea?
Ask for your share of the fellowship's goods
Ask for your pilot's tenth
Ask for the king's peace on Ohthere's ships and your own

The king buys every tooth and all the rope, at the goldsmith's second price. Half is yours by the hand-clasp at the Heaths. The reeve is told your ship pays no toll at the hythe, and Ohthere says that if you lay goods with him again he will not count them twice.

The king buys every tooth and all the rope, and Ohthere counts your tenth out on the board himself, to the penny, with the king watching. The reeve is told your ship pays no toll at the hythe. The clerk is still writing when you leave.

The king says that is the first thing anyone has asked him all week that costs him nothing and is worth having. It is granted, for both houses, in his day. Ohthere pays your pilotage in teeth, the thick ones, and a little silver he says is for the oath.
Whose story
You stand before the king with the teeth and a year of another man's words in your head. The clerk has his pen ready. The king asks how far north the land goes, and then he asks who saw it.
You tell it well. Three days, and three days, and the land bending east. Were you in the ship?
Which hand was the land on when it turned south? A man who was there does not stop to think.
Ohthere is sitting on his own thwart off the hythe, a bowshot from this hall, mending a strap.
A year ago you asked the reeve to make you the man who brings the teeth. He is standing by the door, and he remembers it.
Say that Ohthere saw it, and you only carry it
Say that you were in the ship
Ask leave to bring the Northman in on your own oath

You say whose eyes it was. The king nods, and the clerk writes 'Ohthere said' at the head of the leaf, and you tell it as he told it, days and hands. The king buys the teeth, pays your carrying, and frees your ship of toll at the hythe.

You have heard it so often that the hands come right. The king pays like a king and names you his man for the teeth. On the way out you hear him tell the clerk to leave it out of the book: the man knew the price of everything he had seen. Off the hythe a ship from the north is hoisting her sail.

You stop to think. The clerk puts down his pen. The king, quite mildly, has the reeve go down to the hythe and bring up whoever is sitting there. You are paid for the carrying, and you stand by the door while Ohthere tells it, and nobody looks at you.
The king says he would rather have the hunter than the tale of the hunter, and gives you two days. You go down to the hythe to tell a man who is mending a strap that he is wanted after all.
Tooth for the altar

Cologne was burned by Northmen not many years back and is building again. The archbishop's carver works in a shed against the cathedral wall. He is planing the old figures off a tablet older than the city's walls remember, because he has nothing new to cut.
This was a consul's writing tablet once, in the Romans' time. I take a heathen off it and put a saint on. Every year the tablets get thinner, and so do the saints.
And this is from a whale that walks? I do not care if it is from a cow. It cuts like the true thing. The white is thin. I can work in thin. I have had practice.
Northmen's goods, in this city. The archbishop will ask whether it was hunted or stolen. Hunted is acceptable.
You meant it for the English king, and he is dead. Kings die. Altars need covering every year.
Bring me ten pairs a year, and I keep a man in this city to hold them for you. Or sell me these and be gone. Or give the best pair to Saint Peter, and see what the archbishop gives back.
Agree to bring ten pairs a year
Sell your own teeth at the carver's price
Give the best pair to Saint Peter's altar

The clerk writes it and the carver makes his mark under it with the point of a graver. Your share is counted out in good pennies. A man of the archbishop's household will keep your chests in the city from now on, and the carver puts the consul's tablet back on the shelf with some respect.

They were your teeth and the carver knows it, so he pays what a thing is worth when nobody else has one. The archbishop's man will keep your chests here, and the Frisian at the Heaths sends word that the plot beside his is yours if you mean to do this again.

The best pair goes on the altar on a white cloth. The archbishop's answer comes next morning: a fair price for the rest, and a writing that says the bearer is Saint Peter's man and to be let alone on the river. The carver is already drawing on the tooth with a nail.
The king's share

A year on, the steward at the king's farm has a shed full of teeth and rope that came down the coast in the king's name. Ohthere's ship did not come with it. The steward has not forgotten who told him what it was worth.
The king was pleased. He said a tribute nobody counts is a tribute somebody else is spending.
The Halogalander still has his deer. He has the king's leave to keep them. He does not have leave to sell the Finnas' rope.
The king wants a man who knows the southern markets. He gives silver and his friendship to such a man. Or one of his own ships, sound, eighteen winters old. Which?
Or if your conscience is sore, say so. I will show you the sound and its rocks, and you may sail it without paying me, and we say no more about the Halogalander's share.
On the ridge above the farm the old ship mounds stand in the grass. The men in them took their due from this sound as well.
Carry the king's teeth south each year
Take the ship
Ask that Ohthere keep the selling of his own share

The steward counts out the king's thanks and gives you a tally for eight pairs against next summer. You are the king's guest on this coast now, and may say so. North of here there is a man with six hundred deer who also knows your name.

She lies on the rollers below the farm: clinker, pine above and oak below, a patch at the turn of the bilge and nothing else to say against her. The steward adds a purse so that you can rig her. It is hide rope in the shed, as it happens, and it is the king's.

The steward looks at you as at a man who has sold a horse and wants to pay for its hay. Then he shrugs. Ohthere may sell his own share at his own risk, and the king's goes by the king's men. He pays you the king's thanks all the same, and takes you through the sound at slack water, rock by rock.
The king's book

A priest who copies books for the king has a quire open on his desk: the history of the world by Orosius, put into English. Where the old Roman had little to say about the north, something has been added, or has not.
'Ohthere said to his lord, King Alfred, that he lived northmost of all Northmen.' It goes on for three leaves. Teeth, rope, deer, what the Finnas owe, the days to the Heaths.
No. It does not say who brought him. It does not name his ship either. The book is about the world, not about who held the door.
Here Wulfstan tells of the Este and his seven days to Truso. Of the far north the book says what the Romans said: that it is waste, and cold, and that is all.
A merchant told the king a tale of the north once, with teeth to show for it. The king had it left out. He said the man knew the price of everything he had seen.
They say the carvers at Cologne have a new white tooth to cut. Nobody here has seen it. It would be a fine thing for the boards of a book like this.
The king of the Northmen sells teeth now, I am told, through his stewards. Stewards do not tell stories. It is a pity. The king would have liked to hear one.
Pay for a copy of the seafarer's leaves
Ask for the passage on a leaf, with your name at the foot
Thank him and go down to the ship

He copies Wulfstan's voyage for you in a clear hand, the lands to starboard and the lands to port, and blots it with sand. He says seamen are easy to copy. They never use a long word where a wind will do.

He will not put a mark in the king's book. But he writes the opening of the passage on a clean leaf, and at the foot, small, that a merchant of your house brought the Northman over the sea. He says the foot of a leaf is where the truth usually ends up.
He turns the leaf back and bends to his ruling. Down at the hythe the tide is making, and nobody there has read a book or needs to.
A Frisian has shown the reeve at London a tooth as long as a man's forearm, from a small whale the heathen men hunt north of all dwellings. The goldsmiths are asking where more can be had.
At the king's farm on the Karmsund the steward held a ship of Halogaland with the Finnas' tribute aboard, and asked whose it was to sell.
This year a Northman from the far north sat with King Alfred and told him how the land lies and who lives there. The king had it written down, and bought his teeth.
A Frisian merchant has brought the king whale's teeth from the north and is to bring more each year. He says he has sailed further north than any man.
The archbishop's carver at Cologne has a new white tooth from the north to work, and a Frisian house brings it up the Rhine.
The tribute of the Finnas comes down the coast in King Harald's name now, and his steward on the Karmsund sells the teeth.

A timber jetty at Skiringssal on a grey late-summer afternoon: a tall weather-dark Northman of fifty in a marten cloak stands over a row of long yellow tusks and coils of dark hide rope laid on the planks, his pine-built ship behind him, the wooded shore of the Vik beyond.

Inside a boat shed, light falling through the open seaward end: the tribute laid out by kind on the sand, marten skins, a bear skin, sacks of down, reindeer hides, coils of rope; Ohthere holds one end of a hide rope and the merchant pulls on the other.

A comb-maker's open-fronted shed at Sliesthorp in low morning light, antler offcuts ankle-deep on the floor: a Danish craftsman holds a walrus tusk up to the light with both hands to show its broken end, a small folding scale on the bench beside his saw.

A table under a lean-to against London's old Roman wall, an overcast day: one long tusk lies on the board between an English reeve with a staff and a tonsured clerk bending close to it, the Thames and beached boats seen through a gap in the wall.

A small open boat heeled under a sudden squall in bright hard light: the yard hanging askew from a stranded halyard at the masthead, the crew looking up, and one man's hand on a dark coil of hide rope under the thwart.

The beach below the king's farm on the Karmsund at midsummer evening: a northern ship drawn up with a bare mast, two men carrying her rolled sail up the slope, a steward with an arm ring barring the way to Ohthere, and two grassed ship mounds on the ridge behind.

Open water among low Danish islands at dawn, a light breeze: a long ship under twenty oars coming out from behind an island toward two laden trading hulls, a man in the nearer hull holding a spear up flat as a signal.

The jetties at the head of the Schlei on a clear evening: Ohthere and an English skipper with a string of rough amber sit on chests with ale horns, two roped chests of tusks between them, a Frisian in a short cloak waiting a few paces off with a scale in his hand.

The hythe inside London's river wall on a windy morning: Ohthere's ship lying off on a line, he himself seated on a thwart; on the shingle a priest with a small cross raised, a reeve, and the merchant between them with one hand lifted to swear.

A timber hall by firelight: a slight, intent king in his forties leaning forward over a board where tusks and a coil of rope lie, Ohthere standing before him counting on his fingers, a clerk at the king's elbow with his pen stopped above the leaf, the merchant at the edge of the light.

The same hall by day, shutters open on the river: the merchant alone before the king with two chests of tusks, the clerk looking up with his pen ready, the reeve by the door; through the door, small and far off, a ship at the hythe with one man sitting in her.

A carver's shed built against the wall of Cologne cathedral, scaffolding and new timber above, noon light: an old Frankish carver with a plane in one hand and a worn Roman ivory tablet in the other stares at a walrus tusk on his bench, a clerk behind him with a wax tablet.

A storehouse door standing open at the king's farm on the Karmsund, a bright cold day a year later: tusks stacked like firewood and rope hanging in coils inside, the steward counting silver onto a barrel head, an old clinker ship on rollers below and the two mounds on the ridge.

A copying desk by a small window in winter light: an English priest with ink-stained fingers holds a quire open and points to a line with his pen, the merchant, older now, reading over his shoulder, a ruled blank leaf and a pot of sand at the desk's edge.
